title: El ascensor de los tal vez

lines.text: AUDIO MYSTERY: El ascensor de los tal vez. Opening sound: an elevator arrives on a floor that has no number. A restrained thriller soundtrack hums beneath dialogue.

lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: Elena enters an empty office building carrying a file with four handwritten words: before, after, maybe and never. The elevator doors open without anyone pressing a button. Inside is a brass plaque: The Floor You Heard.

lines.speaker: ELENA
lines.text: Is this a dream?

lines.speaker: VOICE ON INTERCOM
lines.text: Only if you are sure.

lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: The intercom tells her that a witness may have seen a red truck. The voice has a warm accent but no identifiable source. Elena asks, “May have seen, or did see?” The floor indicator flickers between 5 and 15.

lines.speaker: VOICE ON INTERCOM
lines.text: Choose the sentence that you actually heard, not the one that feels complete.
First choice: preserve “might have seen” or announce the person saw it with certainty. Both change the elevator's path. A careful listener can return and compare.

lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: On the next floor, a clinician says a fictional patient has not had a symptom today. In one recording a tiny negation vanishes. The elevator doors are different colors, but the player must rely on sound; no icon gives away the answer.

lines.speaker: ELENA
lines.text: Not having a symptom and having a symptom are not the same story.

lines.speaker: VOICE ON INTERCOM
lines.text: True. But does the interpreter know enough to replace what was said?

lines.speaker: ELENA
lines.text: No. If the words are unclear, the interpreter should disclose the difficulty and request clarification.
Second choice: admit hearing difficulty or invent a plausible answer. The hall beyond each opens onto a different recorded memory.

lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: A third voice, which Elena recognizes as her own, says, “A hearing is scheduled for Tuesday.” Then another version announces the judge has already made a decision. The building shakes as if certainty were a weight on its beams.

lines.speaker: ELENA
lines.text: A scheduled proceeding isn't the same as a ruling. Stop the recording.
Third choice: mark the procedural difference or follow a misleading summary. No gory outcome; the world simply becomes less reliable.

lines.speaker: VOICE ON INTERCOM
lines.text: You made the building more honest. That does not mean you decided what happened.

lines.speaker: ELENA
lines.text: I only kept what was actually said.

Endings: the elevator arrives at a quiet library where the sentences can be heard in their original forms, or loops back to the same floor with a new invitation to listen again. None of the fictional consequences count as evidence of real legal knowledge.

lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: In the building that remembers every word, the only way out is to refuse the words you never heard.

Afterword — The elevator returns in the listener's imagination. The narrator names the four doors without revealing which option to choose. Elena hears a grandmother say in Spanish, “Tal vez no,” and this time the building waits rather than filling in the silence.

lines.speaker: ELENA
lines.text: A pause may be uncomfortable, but a false certainty can reshape what follows.

lines.speaker: VOICE ON INTERCOM
lines.text: What if you don't know which word you heard?

lines.speaker: ELENA
lines.text: Then I ask for it again. The corridor can remain a corridor for another minute.

lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: Outside the window, city buses are still taking people home. The ordinary world looks strange enough when everyone stops guessing what other people must have meant.
Soft door chime, then silence. Credits identify the fiction and the source concepts behind it.
